tagline: Where the Sahara meets the Atlantic
overview:
Morocco stands at Africa's northwest corner, close enough to Europe that on a clear day Spain is visible across the Strait of Gibraltar, just 14 kilometers of water. The country is a little larger than California, with coasts on both the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea, snow-capped mountains through the middle, and the Sahara Desert spreading across the south and east.

About 38 million people live in Morocco. Arabic and Berber, which its speakers call Tamazight, are the official languages, and French is widely used in business and schools. Rabat is the capital, Casablanca the biggest city and busiest port, while Marrakesh, Fez, and Meknes are old imperial cities of palaces, mosques, and walled medinas. Morocco is a kingdom, governed by a king together with an elected parliament.

Morocco also administers Western Sahara to the south, a disputed territory it largely controls and whose status the United Nations considers unresolved.
landAndNature: Three mountain ranges cross the country: the Rif above the Mediterranean, the Middle Atlas with its cedar forests, and the High Atlas, where Toubkal reaches 4,167 meters, the highest peak in North Africa and snowy enough for skiing. South and east of the Atlas the land dries into stony plains, palm-filled oases, and the dunes of Erg Chebbi, some more than 100 meters tall. Rivers such as the Draa run down from the mountains and vanish into sand. Barbary macaques, the only monkeys living wild north of the Sahara, swing through the cedars, while fennec foxes hunt in the desert. Off the Atlantic coast, cold currents feed huge shoals of sardines.
peopleAndCulture: Moroccans are mostly Arab and Amazigh (Berber), and many speak Darija, the Moroccan form of Arabic, at home; Amazigh has its own alphabet, Tifinagh, which appears on road signs. Nearly everyone is Muslim, and the call to prayer marks out the day. The food is famous: tagines slow-cooked in cone-lidded clay pots, couscous served on Fridays, harira soup, and sweet mint tea poured from high above the glass. Each evening storytellers, musicians, and food stalls take over the Jemaa el-Fna square in Marrakesh. Gnawa musicians play iron castanets and a three-stringed guembri at festivals in Essaouira. Soccer is the national sport, and in 2022 Morocco became the first African team to reach a World Cup semifinal.
history: Amazigh peoples have lived in North Africa for thousands of years. Phoenicians and then Romans built ports along the coast, and the Roman ruins of Volubilis still stand near Meknes. Arab armies brought Islam in the late 600s, and from Fez, founded around 789, a series of Moroccan dynasties ruled; the Almoravids and Almohads at their height governed an empire stretching into Spain. Morocco kept its independence while much of Africa fell to European powers, until France and Spain imposed protectorates in 1912. Nationalists and the sultan pressed for freedom, and independence came in 1956 under Mohammed V. The Alaouite dynasty, on the throne since the 1600s, still reigns, and a new constitution in 2011 shifted some powers to the elected parliament.
funFacts: The University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, founded in 859, is recognized as the oldest continuously operating university in the world.
The medina of Fez has thousands of narrow alleys and no cars; goods still move by donkey and handcart.
Goats really do climb argan trees in southwestern Morocco to reach the fruit, sometimes six or seven in a single tree.
The Noor solar complex near Ouarzazate uses curved mirrors spread over thousands of hectares to concentrate desert sunlight into power.
Casablanca's Hassan II Mosque stands partly over the Atlantic and has one of the tallest minarets on Earth, 210 meters high.
